protoceratops:eswiki:10.title: Protoceratops (Teoría sobre el origen del mito del grifo)

facts.statement: The genus Protoceratops was described by Granger and Gregory in 1923.
facts.quote: authority: Granger & Gregory, 1923

facts.statement: Protoceratops lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 75 to 71 million years ago.
facts.quote: lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous, around 75 to 71 million years ago

facts.statement: Adult Protoceratops were small ceratopsians reaching up to 2.5 meters in length and weighing between 62 and 104 kilograms.
facts.quote: Protoceratops were small ceratopsians, up to 2 - 2.5 m long and around 62 - 104 kg in body mass

facts.statement: While adult Protoceratops were primarily quadrupedal, juveniles could walk bipedally if needed.
facts.quote: While adults were largely quadrupedal, juveniles had the capacity to walk around bipedally if necessary

facts.statement: Protoceratops were characterized by a large skull, a short stiff neck, and a prominent neck frill.
facts.quote: They were characterized by a proportionally large skull, short and stiff neck, and neck frill

facts.statement: The neck frill likely served for display, intraspecific combat, neck protection, and anchoring jaw muscles.
facts.quote: The frill was likely used for display or intraspecific combat, as well as protection of the neck and anchoring of jaw muscles

facts.statement: Protoceratops possessed a nose horn that was single in P. andrewsi but double in P. hellenikorhinus.
facts.quote: A horn-like structure was present over the nose, which varied from a single structure in P. andrewsi to a double, paired structure in P. hellenikorhinus

facts.statement: Protoceratops forelimbs had five fingers, with only the first three bearing wide, flat claws.
facts.quote: The forelimbs had five fingers of which only the first three bore wide and flat unguals

facts.statement: Protoceratops feet were wide with four toes featuring flattened, shovel-like claws adapted for digging in sand.
facts.quote: The feet were wide and had four toes with flattened, shovel-like unguals, which would have been useful for digging through the sand

facts.statement: Protoceratops had a long tail with an enigmatic sail-like structure possibly used for display, swimming, or thermoregulation.
facts.quote: The tail was long and had an enigmatic sail-like structure, which may have been used for display, swimming, or metabolic reasons

facts.statement: Protoceratops were herbivores with jaws and teeth adapted for chopping foliage and plant material.
facts.quote: Protoceratops, like many other ceratopsians, were herbivores equipped with prominent jaws and teeth suited for chopping foliage and other plant material

facts.statement: Protoceratops appear to have cared for their young and laid soft-shelled eggs, a rare trait among dinosaurs.
facts.quote: They appear to have cared for their young. They laid soft-shelled eggs, a rare occurrence in dinosaurs

facts.statement: Protoceratops were hunted by Velociraptor, evidenced by the famous 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen showing a Protoceratops locked in combat.
facts.quote: Protoceratops were hunted by Velociraptor, and one particularly famous specimen (the Fighting Dinosaurs) preserves a pair of them locked in combat

facts.statement: Protoceratops are now thought to be cathemeral (active at dawn and dusk), replacing earlier beliefs that they were nocturnal based on their large scleral rings.
facts.quote: Protoceratops used to be characterized as nocturnal because of the large scleral ring around the eye, but they are now thought to have been cathemeral (active at dawn and dusk)

facts.statement: In 1923, the Central Asiatic Expedition discovered more Protoceratops fossils along with the first remains of Oviraptor, Saurornithoides, and Velociraptor.
facts.quote: In 1923 the expedition again prospected the Flaming Cliffs, this time discovering even more specimens of Protoceratops and also the first remains of Oviraptor, Saurornithoides and Velociraptor

facts.statement: The Tugriken Shireh locality has yielded significant Protoceratops specimens, including the 'Fighting Dinosaurs', standing individuals, authentic nests, and herd-like groups.
facts.quote: Since its discovery, the Tugriken Shireh locality has yielded some of the most significant specimens of Protoceratops, such as the Fighting Dinosaurs, in situ individuals—a preservation condition also known as "standing" individuals or specimens in some cases—, authentic nests, and small herd-like groups

facts.statement: It is debated whether Protoceratops was an ancestor of ankylosaurians and larger ceratopsians like Triceratops, as this view changed with further discoveries.
facts.quote: Protoceratops was initially believed to be an ancestor of ankylosaurians and larger ceratopsians, such as Triceratops and relatives, until the discoveries of other protoceratopsids

facts.statement: Protoceratops fossils are often found in excellent preservation, including delicate scleral rings, making it one of the best-known Asian dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Most fossils were in an excellent state of preservation with even scleral rings (delicate ocular bones) preserved in some specimens, quickly making Protoceratops one of the best-known dinosaurs from Asia

facts.statement: Protoceratops remains were found in the 1970s in Mongolia by Polish-Mongolian expeditions.
facts.quote: Protoceratopsid remains were recovered in the 1970s from the Khulsan locality of the Barun Goyot Formation, Mongolia, during the work of several Polish-Mongolian paleontological expeditions.

facts.statement: In 1975, Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska described the species Protoceratops kozlowskii.
facts.quote: In 1975, Polish paleontologists Teresa Maryańska and Halszka Osmólska described a second species of Protoceratops which they named P. kozlowskii.

facts.statement: Oliver Lambert and colleagues named the species Protoceratops hellenikorhinus in 2001.
facts.quote: In 2001 Oliver Lambert with colleagues named a new and distinct species of Protoceratops, P. hellenikorhinus.

facts.statement: Remains of P. hellenikorhinus were collected in Inner Mongolia in 1995 and 1996 by Sino-Belgian expeditions.
facts.quote: The first known remains of P. hellenikorhinus were collected from the Bayan Mandahu locality of the Bayan Mandahu Formation, Inner Mongolia, in 1995 and 1996 during Sino-Belgian paleontological expeditions.

facts.statement: Konstantin E. Mikhailov named the egg genus Protoceratopsidovum in 1994, linking it to Protoceratops.
facts.quote: In 1994 the Russian paleontologist Konstantin E. Mikhailov named the new oogenus Protoceratopsidovum from the Barun Goyot and Djadokhta formations, with the type species P. sincerum and additional P. fluxuosum and P. minimum.

facts.statement: A fossil known as the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' shows a Protoceratops and a Velociraptor preserved together in combat.
facts.quote: The Fighting Dinosaurs specimen preserves a Protoceratops (MPC-D 100/512) and Velociraptor (MPC-D 100/25) fossilized in combat and provides an important window regarding direct evidence of predator-prey behavior in non-avian dinosaurs.

facts.statement: The 'Fighting Dinosaurs' fossils were discovered on August 3 at the Tugriken Shire locality in the Djadokhta Formation.
facts.quote: During fieldwork on 3 August several fossils of Protoceratops and Velociraptor were found at the Tugriken Shire locality (Djadokhta Formation) including a block containing one of each.

facts.statement: It is debated how the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' died, with drowning considered unlikely due to the arid environment.
facts.quote: Though a drowning scenario has been proposed by Barsbold, such a hypothesis is considered unlikely given the arid paleoenvironments of the Djadokhta Formation.

facts.statement: Most researchers believe the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' were buried alive by a sandstorm or a collapsing dune.
facts.quote: It is generally thought that they were buried alive by a sandstorm or a collapsed dune.

facts.statement: A nearly complete Protoceratops skeleton was collected at the Flaming Cliffs during the Third Central Asiatic Expedition in 1923.
facts.quote: During the Third Central Asiatic Expedition in 1923, a nearly complete Protoceratops skeleton (specimen AMNH 6418) was collected at the Flaming Cliffs.

facts.statement: A fossilized footprint of a four-toed digitigrade dinosaur was found beneath the pelvic girdle of a Protoceratops skeleton in the 2000s.
facts.quote: In the 2000s during the preparation of the specimen, a fossilized cast of a four-toed digitigrade footprint was found below the pelvic girdle.

facts.statement: A footprint associated with an articulated Protoceratops skeleton was first reported in 2012 by Niedźwiedzki and colleagues.
facts.quote: This footprint was described in 2012 by Grzegorz Niedźwiedzki and colleagues who considered it to represent one of the first reported finds of a dinosaur footprint in association with an articulated skeleton, and also the first one reported for Protoceratops.

facts.statement: Protoceratops species were small ceratopsians, measuring between 2 and 2.5 meters in length and weighing between 62 and 104 kilograms.
facts.quote: Protoceratops was a relatively small-sized ceratopsian, with both P. andrewsi and P. hellenikorhinus estimated up to 2 - 2.5 m in length, and around 62 - 104 kg in body mass.

facts.statement: P. andrewsi is characterized by two premaxillary teeth, a low and long snout, a single pointed nasal horn, and a slightly curved dentary edge.
facts.quote: P. andrewsi – Two teeth were present at the premaxilla; the snout was low and long; the nasal horn was a single, pointed structure; the bottom edge of the dentary was slightly curved.

facts.statement: P. hellenikorhinus lacks premaxillary teeth, has a tall and broad snout, a nasal horn divided into two ridges, and a straight dentary edge.
facts.quote: P. hellenikorhinus – Absence of premaxillary teeth; the snout was tall and broad; the nasal horn was divided into two pointed ridges; the bottom edge of the dentary was straight.

facts.statement: The skull of P. hellenikorhinus had a total length of about 70 centimeters.
facts.quote: On the other hand P. hellenikorhinus had a total skull length of about 70 cm.

facts.statement: Protoceratops had a pronounced neck frill composed mainly of parietal and squamosal bones.
facts.quote: The rear of the skull gave form to a pronounced neck frill (also known as "parietal frill") mostly composed of the parietal and squamosal bones.

facts.statement: The epijugal region of the skull was covered by a horny sheath.
facts.quote: The surfaces around the epijugal were coarse, indicating that it was covered by a horny sheath.

facts.statement: Protoceratops lacked horn cores or supraorbital horns on its frontal and postorbital bones.
facts.quote: The frontal and postorbital bones of Protoceratops were flat and lacked horn cores or supraorbital horns.

facts.statement: In P. hellenikorhinus, the palpebral bone created a small horn-like structure above the eye socket.
facts.quote: In P. hellenikorhinus the palpebral protruded upwards from the prefrontal, just above the orbit and slightly meeting the frontal, creating a small horn-like structure.

facts.statement: The scleral ring inside the orbit was circular and formed by consecutive bony plates.
facts.quote: The scleral ring (structure that supports the eyeball), found inside the orbit, was circular in shape and formed by consecutive bony plates.

facts.statement: Protoceratops had large orbits measuring around 5 centimeters in diameter.
facts.quote: Protoceratops had large orbits, which measured around 5 cm in diameter and had irregular shapes depending on the individual.

facts.statement: Protoceratops had well-developed binocular vision due to its forward-facing, closely located orbits and narrow snout.
facts.quote: The forward facing and closely located orbits combined with a narrow snout, gave Protoceratops a well-developed binocular vision.

facts.statement: The rostral bone was toothless, triangular, and textured to support a horny beak.
facts.quote: The rostral bone was devoid of teeth, high and triangular in shape. It had a sharp end and rough texture, which reflects that a rhamphotheca (horny beak) was present.

facts.statement: Protoceratops had leaf-shaped teeth with serrated edges.
facts.quote: Protoceratops had leaf-shaped dentary and maxillary teeth that bore several denticles (serrations) on their respective edges.

facts.statement: Protoceratops teeth were packed in a single row to create a shearing surface.
facts.quote: The teeth were packed into a single row that created a shearing surface.

facts.statement: P. andrewsi had two small peg-like teeth on the underside of each premaxilla.
facts.quote: P. andrewsi bore two small, peg to spike-like teeth that were located on the underside of each premaxilla.

facts.statement: The premaxillary teeth of Protoceratops lacked denticles and had a smooth surface.
facts.quote: Unlike dentary and maxillary teeth, the premaxillary dentition was devoid of denticles, having a relatively smooth surface.

facts.statement: All teeth of Protoceratops had a single root.
facts.quote: All teeth had a single root (lower part inserted in the alveoli).

facts.statement: Protoceratops possessed a vertebral column consisting of nine neck vertebrae, twelve back vertebrae, eight pelvic vertebrae, and more than forty tail vertebrae.
facts.quote: The vertebral column of Protoceratops had nine cervical (neck), 12 dorsal (back), eight sacral (pelvic) and over 40 caudal (tail) vertebrae.

facts.statement: The neck of Protoceratops was short and lacked flexibility.
facts.quote: The neck was rather short and had poor flexibility.

facts.statement: The mid-section of Protoceratops' tail featured elongated neural spines that formed a sail-like structure.
facts.quote: The caudal vertebrae decreased in size progressively towards the end and had very elongated neural spines in the mid-series, forming a sail-like structure.

facts.statement: Protoceratops had chevrons attached to its tail, with the largest ones located between the third and ninth caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: The first chevron was located at the union of the third and fourth caudals. Chevrons three to nine were the largest and from the tenth onwards they became smaller.

facts.statement: Protoceratops had forelimbs that were shorter than its hindlimbs.
facts.quote: The forelimbs of Protoceratops were shorted than the hindlimbs, and composed by the humerus, radius, and ulna.

facts.statement: Protoceratops' hands had five fingers, with the first three bearing large claws and the last two being small and vestigial.
facts.quote: The manus (hand) of Protoceratops had five digits (fingers). The first three fingers had unguals (claw bones) and were the largest digits. The last two were devoid of unguals and had a small size, mostly vestigial (retained, but without important function).

facts.statement: The claws on both the hands and feet of Protoceratops were flat, blunt, and hoof-like in shape.
facts.quote: Both hand and feet unguals were flat, blunt and hoof-like.

facts.statement: Protoceratops' feet had four toes equipped with shovel-like claws.
facts.quote: The pes (foot) were composed of four metatarsal and four toes which bore shovel-like pedal unguals.

facts.statement: Granger and Gregory established the family Protoceratopsidae in 1923 with Protoceratops as its representative species.
facts.quote: Protoceratops was in 1923 placed within the newly named family Protoceratopsidae as the representative species by Granger and Gregory.

facts.statement: In 1925, Gregory and Charles C. Mook concluded that Protoceratops was a primitive ceratopsian rather than an ancestor to ankylosaurs.
facts.quote: Gregory and Charles C. Mook in 1925 upon a more deeper analysis of Protoceratops and its overall morphology, concluded that this taxon represents a ceratopsian more primitive than ceratopsids and not an ankylosaur-ceratopsian ancestor.

facts.statement: Edwin H. Colbert suggested in 1951 that Protoceratops was a key ancestor for large ceratopsians like Styracosaurus and Triceratops.
facts.quote: In 1951 Edwin H. Colbert considered Protoceratops to represent a key ancestor for the ceratopsid lineage, suggesting that it ultimately led to the evolution of large-bodied ceratopsians such as Styracosaurus and Triceratops.

facts.statement: Maryanska and Osmolska argued in 1975 that Protoceratopsids likely did not evolve from Psittacosaurids nor give rise to advanced Ceratopsids.
facts.quote: However, in 1975 Maryanska and Osmolska argued that it is very unlikely that protoceratopsids evolved from psittacosaurids, and also unlikely that they gave rise to the highly derived (advanced) ceratopsids.

facts.statement: Paul Sereno formally defined the family Protoceratopsidae in 1998 as a clade of coronosaurs closer to Protoceratops than to Triceratops.
facts.quote: In 1998, paleontologist Paul Sereno formally defined Protoceratopsidae as the branch-based clade including all coronosaurs closer to Protoceratops than to Triceratops.

facts.statement: Modern phylogenetic analyses often recover Protoceratops and Bagaceratops as sister taxa, rejecting links to more derived ceratopsians.
facts.quote: In most recent/modern phylogenetic analyses Protoceratops and Bagaceratops are commonly recovered as sister taxa, leaving the interpretations proposing direct relationships with more derived ceratopsians unsupported.

facts.statement: Recent analysis suggests the family Protoceratopsidae consists of the genera Bagaceratops, Breviceratops, and Protoceratops.
facts.quote: Under this reasoning, Protoceratopsidae consists of Bagaceratops, Breviceratops, and Protoceratops.

facts.statement: Protoceratopsids are characterized by primitive morphology, lacking well-developed horn cores and having smaller body sizes compared to derived Ceratopsids.
facts.quote: This family was characterized by their overall primitive morphology in comparison to the more derived Ceratopsidae, such as lack of well-developed horn cores and relative smaller body size.

facts.statement: In 2010, Longrich and colleagues suggested P. hellenikorhinus may represent a lineage with a longer evolutionary history or a direct descendant of P. andrewsi.
facts.quote: Longrich and team in 2010 indicated that highly derived morphology of P. hellenikorhinus—when compared to P. andrewsi—indicates that this species may represent a lineage of Protoceratops that had a longer evolutionary history compared to P. andrewsi, or simply a direct descendant of P. andrewsi.

facts.statement: Morphological differences between Protoceratops species suggest the Bayan Mandahu Formation is slightly younger than the Djadokhta Formation.
facts.quote: The difference in morphologies between Protoceratops also suggests that the nearby Bayan Mandahu Formation is slightly younger than the Djadokhta Formation.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the large neck frill of Protoceratops likely served as an attachment site for jaw muscles to help anchor the lower jaws during feeding.
facts.quote: He suggested that the large neck frill was likely an attachment site for masticatory muscles.

facts.statement: Studies of enamel microstructure concluded that the shape of Protoceratops teeth did not relate to diet or food processing in the same way it does for most animals.
facts.quote: They concluded that enamel shape does not relate to the diet or function of the teeth as most animals do not necessarily use teeth to process food.

facts.statement: The coarsely textured enamel and micro-serrations on Protoceratops teeth likely helped crumble vegetation, making their feeding method more efficient than in other groups.
facts.quote: This feeding method was likely more efficient in protoceratopsids as the enamel surface of Protoceratops was coarsely-textured and the tips of the micro-serrations developed on the basis of the teeth, probably helping to crumble vegetation.

facts.statement: The neck frill of Protoceratops changed dramatically from a small, flat structure in juveniles to a large, fan-like structure in fully mature individuals.
facts.quote: The neck frill specifically, underwent a dramatic change from a small, flat, and almost rounded structure in juveniles to a large, fan-like one in fully mature Protoceratops individuals.

facts.statement: Makovicky and team conducted a 2007 histological analysis of Protoceratops fossils from the American Museum of Natural History to understand its life history.
facts.quote: Makovicky and team in 2007 conducted a histological analysis on several specimens of Protoceratops from the American Museum of Natural History collections to provide insights into the life history of Protoceratops.

facts.statement: Fossil bone analysis indicates Protoceratops slowed its growth around 9 to 10 years of age and ceased growing around 11 to 13 years.
facts.quote: The examined fossil bones indicated that Protoceratops slowed its ontogeny (growth) around 9–10 years of life, and it ceased around 11–13 years.

facts.statement: Makovicky and team stated that because radical changes in the neck frill and nasal horn occur in most adults, distinguishing sexual dimorphism in adult Protoceratops may be difficult.
facts.quote: Makovicky and team also stated that as the maximum/radical changes on the neck frill and nasal horn were present in most adult individuals, trying to differentiate sexual dimorphism (anatomical differences between sexes) in adult Protoceratops may not be a good practice.

facts.statement: David Hone and colleagues found in 2016 that the Protoceratops neck frill was disproportionately small in juveniles, grew rapidly during development, and reached a large size only in adults.
facts.quote: David Hone and colleagues in 2016 upon their analysis of P. andrewsi neck frills, found that the frill of Protoceratops was disproportionally smaller in juveniles, grew at a rapid rate than the rest of the animal during its ontogeny, and reached a considerable size only in large adult individuals.

facts.statement: During growth, Protoceratops exhibited elongation of premaxillary teeth from small in juveniles to enlarged in adults, and taller middle neural spines in the tail as it approached adulthood.
facts.quote: Other changes during ontogeny include the elongation of the premaxillary teeth that are smaller in juveniles and enlarged in adults, and the enlargement of middle neural spines in the tail or caudal vertebrae, which appear to grow much taller when approaching adulthood.

facts.statement: In Protoceratops, the squamosal bone grew larger than the parietal bone from subadult to adult stages, while the frill expanded upward.
facts.quote: From subadult to adult individuals, the squamosal bone increased in size more than the parietal bone, and the frill expanded to a top direction.

facts.statement: Analysis of various bones including the neck frill and limb bones showed that the bone histology of Protoceratops remained uniform throughout its growth.
facts.quote: The sampled elements consisted of neck frill, femur, tibia, fibula, ribs, humerus and radius bones, and showed that the histology of Protoceratops remained rather uniform throughout ontogeny.

facts.statement: Protoceratops bone was characterized by simple fibrolamellar tissue with an irregular fibrous texture, prominent woven fibers, and low bone remodeling.
facts.quote: It was characterized by simple fibrolamellar bone—bony tissue with an irregular, fibrous texture and filled with blood vessels—with prominent woven-fibered bone and low bone remodeling.

facts.statement: Researcher Tereshchenko suggested in 1996 that Protoceratops was likely an obligate quadruped based on its limb proportions.
facts.quote: In 1996, Tereshchenko reconstructed the walking model of Protoceratops where he considered the most likely scenario to be Protoceratops as an obligate quadruped given the proportions of its limbs.

facts.statement: Protoceratops likely used a trot-like gait primarily with its hindlimbs and probably did not use an asymmetric gait.
facts.quote: The main gait of Protoceratops was probably trot-like mostly using its hindlimbs and it is unlikely to have used an asymmetric gait.

facts.statement: Protoceratops could have used rapid, optional bipedalism when trapped in dangerous situations or while foraging.
facts.quote: If trapped in a specific situation (like danger or foraging), Protoceratops could have employed a rapid, facultative bipedalism.

facts.statement: The flat and wide toe claws of Protoceratops likely allowed it to walk efficiently on loose sand.
facts.quote: He also noted that the flat and wide pedal unguals of Protoceratops may have allowed efficient walking through loose terrain, such as sand which was common on its surroundings.

facts.statement: Tereshchenko estimated the maximum walking speed of Protoceratops to be about 3 km/h.
facts.quote: Tereshchenko using speed equations also estimated the average maximum walking speed of Protoceratops at about 3 km/h (kilometres per hour).

facts.statement: Protoceratops forelimbs could sprawl laterally but were tucked in for quadrupedal movement.
facts.quote: The forelimbs of Protoceratops could sprawl laterally but not for quadrupedal locomotion, which was accomplished with the elbows tucked in.

facts.statement: Kuznetsov and Tereshchenko concluded in 2010 that Protoceratops had greater lateral mobility in its pre-hip vertebrae and reduced vertical mobility in its neck.
facts.quote: In 2010 Alexander Kuznetsov and Tereshchenko analyzed several vertebrae series of Protoceratops to estimate overall mobility, and concluded that Protoceratops had greater lateral mobility in the presacral (pre-hip) vertebrae series and reduced vertical mobility in the cervical (neck) region.

facts.statement: Footprints from specimen ZPAL Mg D-II/3 described by Niedźwiedzki in 2012 show that Protoceratops walked digitigrade, supporting its weight on its toes.
facts.quote: The fossilized footprint associated with the specimen ZPAL Mg D-II/3 described by Niedźwiedzki in 2012 indicates that Protoceratops was digitigrade, meaning that it walked with its toes supporting the body weight.

facts.statement: Słowiak and team found in 2019 that a sub-adult Protoceratops specimen had limb features typical of bipedal ceratopsians.
facts.quote: In 2019 however, Słowiak and team described the limb elements of ZPAL Mg D-II/3, which represents a sub-adult individual, and noted a mix of characters typical of bipedal ceratopsians such as a narrow glenoid with scapular blade and an arched femur.

facts.statement: Young Protoceratops could use facultative bipedalism while adults maintained an obligate quadrupedal stance.
facts.quote: The absence of these traits in mature individuals indicates that young Protoceratops were capable of facultative bipedal locomotion and adults had an obligate quadrupedal stance.

facts.statement: Adult Protoceratops likely could occasionally stand on their hindlimbs despite being stocky quadrupeds, based on their tibia-femur length ratio.
facts.quote: Even though adult Protoceratops were stocky and quadruped, their tibia-femur length ratio—the tibia being longer than femur, a trait present in bipedal ceratopsians—suggests the ability to occasionally stand on their hindlimbs.

facts.statement: Longrich proposed in 2010 that Protoceratops used its hindlimbs to dig burrows or shelter to escape daytime heat.
facts.quote: Longrich in 2010 proposed that Protoceratops may have used its hindlimbs to dig burrows or take shelter under bushes and/or scrapes to escape the hottest temperatures of the day.

facts.statement: Protoceratops hindlimb digging was likely aided by a strong caudofemoralis muscle and flat, shovel-like toe claws.
facts.quote: A digging action with the hindlimbs was likely facilitated by the strong caudofemoralis muscle and its large feet equipped with flat, shovel-like unguals.

facts.statement: Common digging behavior likely caused Protoceratops to become trapped alive in collapsing burrows or sandstorms, explaining some standing fossil postures.
facts.quote: As this behavior would have been common in Protoceratops, it predisposed individuals to become entombed alive during the sudden collapse of their burrows and high energy sand-bearing events—such as sandstorms—and thus explaining the standing in-situ posture of some specimens.

facts.statement: Longrich suggested that backward burrowing explains why some Protoceratops fossils are preserved facing forward with curved tails.
facts.quote: Longrich suggested that a backward burrowing could explain the preservation of some specimens pointing forward with curved tails.

facts.statement: Gregory and Mook suggested in 1925 that Protoceratops was partially aquatic due to its large feet and long tail vertebrae neural spines.
facts.quote: Gregory and Mook in 1925 suggested that Protoceratops was partially aquatic because of its large feet—being larger than the hands—and the very long neural spines found in the caudal (tail) vertebrae.

facts.statement: Brown and Schlaikjer indicated in 1940 that Protoceratops likely used a strong ischiocaudalis muscle and high tail spines for swimming.
facts.quote: Brown and Schlaikjer in 1940 indicated that the expansion of the distal (lower) ischial end may reflect a strong ischiocaudalis muscle, which together with the high tail neural spines were used for swimming.

facts.statement: Bailey disagreed in 1997 with aquatic hypotheses, suggesting the high tail spines were for storing fat and water like desert lizards.
facts.quote: Jack Bowman Bailey in 1997 disagreed with previous aquatic hypotheses and indicated that the high caudal neural spines were instead more reminiscent of bulbous tails of some desert lizard species (such as Heloderma or Uromastyx), which are related to store fat with metabolic water in the tail.

facts.statement: Tereshchenko concluded in 2008 that elevated tail spines were a swimming adaptation based on river sediments and vertebral shapes.
facts.quote: In 2008, based on the occurrence of some Protoceratops specimens in fluvial (river-deposited) sediments from the Djadokhta Formation and heterocoelous (vertebral centra that are saddle-shaped at both ends) caudal vertebrae of protoceratopsids, Tereshchenko concluded that the elevated caudal spines are a swimming adaptation.

facts.statement: Tereshchenko proposed that protoceratopsids used their laterally flattened tails as paddles for swimming.
facts.quote: He proposed that protoceratopsids moved through water using their laterally flattened tails as a paddle to aid in swimming.

facts.statement: Longrich argued in 2010 that the high tail and frill helped Protoceratops shed heat in arid environments.
facts.quote: Longrich in 2010 argued that the high tail and frill of Protoceratops may have helped it to shed excess heat during the day—acting as large-surface structures—when the animal was active in order to survive in the relatively arid environments of the Djadokhta Formation without highly developed cooling mechanisms.

facts.statement: Lee and colleagues found swimming hypotheses hard to prove in 2011 due to Protoceratops fossils found in wind-deposited arid sediments.
facts.quote: In 2011, during the description of Koreaceratops, Yuong-Nam Lee and colleagues found the above swimming hypotheses hard to prove based on the abundance of Protoceratops in eolian (wind-deposited) sediments that were deposited in prominent arid environments.

facts.statement: Tereschenko concluded in 2013 that Protoceratops had adaptations for both terrestrial and aquatic habits.
facts.quote: Tereschhenko in 2013 examined the structure of the caudal vertebrae spines of Protoceratops, concluding that it had adaptations for terrestrial and aquatic habits.

facts.statement: Protoceratops likely raised its tail for display or for females to expand the cloaca during egg laying.
facts.quote: It is likely that Protoceratops raised its tail as a signal (display) or females could use this method during egg laying to expand and relax the cloaca.

facts.statement: Hone and team indicated in 2016 that the Protoceratops tail was used for display to impress mates or for species recognition.
facts.quote: In 2016, Hone and team indicated that the tail of Protoceratops, particularly the mid region with elevated neural spines, could have been used in display to impress potential mates and/or for species recognition.

facts.statement: Kim and team suggested in 2019 that elongated tail spines were well-suited for swimming.
facts.quote: Kim with team in 2019 cited the elongated tail spines as well-suited for swimming.

facts.statement: Kim and team suggested swimming adaptations helped Protoceratops avoid aquatic predators like crocodylomorphs.
facts.quote: The team also suggested that a swimming adaptation could have been useful to avoid aquatic predators, such as crocodylomorphs.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that juvenile Protoceratops aggregated primarily for defense against predators.
facts.quote: Hone and colleagues in particular suggested that juveniles would aggregate primarily as a defense against predators

facts.statement: While evidence supports herd behavior, it remains possible that some Protoceratops individuals lived solitarily.
facts.quote: The team also indicated that, while Protoceratops provides direct evidence for the formation of single cohort aggregations throughout its lifespan, it cannot be ruled out the possibility that some Protoceratops were solitary.

facts.statement: In 2018, Tereshchenko reported abnormally fused cervical vertebrae in a specimen of P. andrewsi, likely caused by disease or external damage.
facts.quote: In 2018, Tereshchenko examined and described several articulated cervical vertebrae of P. andrewsi and reported the presence of two abnormally fused vertebrae

facts.statement: In 1974, Barsbold described the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen showing a Velociraptor pinned under a Protoceratops.
facts.quote: Barsbold in 1974 shortly described the Fighting Dinosaurs specimen and discussed possible scenarios.

facts.statement: In the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen, the Protoceratops bit the Velociraptor's hand, suggesting it was trapped and unable to escape.
facts.quote: The Protoceratops bit the right hand of the predator, implying that it was unable to escape.

facts.statement: In 1993, Osmólska proposed two alternative hypotheses for the preservation of the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen involving a collapsing dune or scavenging.
facts.quote: Osmólska in 1993 proposed another two hypotheses to explain their preservation.

facts.statement: In 1995, Unwin and colleagues disputed the scavenging hypothesis for the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen, suggesting instead that both animals were buried alive by a sandstorm.
facts.quote: In 1995, David M. Unwin and colleagues cast doubt on previous explanations especially a scavenging hypothesis as there were numerous indications of a concurrent death event.

facts.statement: In 1998, Kenneth Carpenter argued that the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen proves theropods were active predators rather than scavengers.
facts.quote: Kenneth Carpenter in 1998 considered the Fighting Dinosaurs specimen to be conclusive evidence for theropods as active predators and not scavengers.

facts.statement: In 2010, David Hone and colleagues reported tooth marks on Protoceratops fossils indicating feeding by Velociraptor.
facts.quote: In 2010, David Hone with team reported a new interaction between Velociraptor and Protoceratops based on tooth marks.

facts.statement: Researchers concluded that Protoceratops was a common part of the Velociraptor diet in these environments.
facts.quote: The team stated that feeding by Velociraptor upon Protoceratops was probably a relatively common occurrence in these environments, and that this ceratopsian actively formed part of the diet of Velociraptor.

facts.statement: In 2016, Barsbold re-examined the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' specimen and found displaced pectoral elements and a torn forelimb.
facts.quote: In 2016, Barsbold re-examined the Fighting Dinosaurs specimen and found several anomalies within the Protoceratops individual

facts.statement: Barsbold suggested scavengers or herd members might have torn off the Protoceratops limbs after burial, though he noted no direct evidence for the latter.
facts.quote: Barsbold suggested that scavengers were the most likely authors. Because Protoceratops is considered to have been a herding animal, another hypothesis is that members of a herd tried to pull out the already buried Protoceratops

facts.statement: The genus Protoceratops was named by Granger and Gregory in 1923.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Granger & Gregory, 1923

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Protoceratops is Protoceratops andrewsi.
facts.quote: type_species: Protoceratops andrewsi

facts.statement: Protoceratops fossils date to the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Cretácico Superior

facts.statement: Protoceratops belongs to the family Protoceratopsidae.
facts.quote: familia: Protoceratopsidae

facts.statement: Protoceratops hellenikorhinus is a species within the genus Protoceratops, described by Lambet and colleagues in 2001.
facts.quote: subdivision: Protoceratops hellenikorhinus Lambet et ál., 2001

facts.statement: Protoceratops was an herbivore about the size of a sheep, measuring between 1.5 and 2 meters in length, and was very abundant in what is now Mongolia.
facts.quote: Con el tamaño de una oveja, entre 1,5 a 2 metros, este herbívoro fue muy abundante en lo que es hoy Mongolia.

facts.statement: Unlike later ceratopsians, Protoceratops lacked well-developed horns and retained some primitive traits not seen in later genera.
facts.quote: A diferencia de los ceratopsianos posteriores careció de cuernos bien desarrollados y conservó algunos rasgos primitivos no vistos en géneros posteriores.

facts.statement: Protoceratops had a large neck frill that likely served for protection, anchoring strong jaw muscles, impressing members of its species, or a combination of these functions.
facts.quote: El Protoceratops poseía una gran gola en el cuello, que le habría servido para protegerse, como punto de anclaje de los fuertes músculos de las mandíbulas, para impresionar a los miembros de su especie o para una combinación de estas funciones.

facts.statement: Protoceratops was first described by Walter Granger and W. K. Gregory in 1923 and was initially considered the direct ancestor of North American ceratopsians.
facts.quote: Descrito por Walter Granger y W. K. Gregory en 1923, fue considerado en un principio como el ancestro directo de los ceratopsianos norteamericanos.

facts.statement: Researchers have recognized two species of Protoceratops, P. andrewsi and P. hellenikorhinus, based partly on their respective sizes.
facts.quote: Con el tiempo los investigadores han reconocido a dos especies de Protoceratops andrewsi y Protoceratops hellenikorhinus, basados en parte en sus respectivos tamaños.

facts.statement: A genuine Protoceratops nest containing newborn remains was not discovered until 2011, suggesting parental care in this dinosaur.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, no sería hasta 2011 que se descubrió un nido de Protoceratops genuino, con los restos de los recién nacidos en su interior sugiriendo el cuidado de los padres en este dinosaurio.

facts.statement: Protoceratops could reach a length of 1.8 meters, a height of 60 centimeters at the hips, and weigh 60 kilograms.
facts.quote: El Protoceratops llegó a medir 1,8 metros de largo, con 60 centímetros de alto hasta la cruz, y a pesar 60 kilogramos.

facts.statement: A fully developed adult Protoceratops would have weighed approximately 82.7 kilograms.
facts.quote: Un adulto completamente desarrollado habría pesado aproximadamente 82,7 kilogramos.

facts.statement: The smallest specimens of Protoceratops are estimated to have weighed 23.7 kilograms.
facts.quote: Los especímenes más pequeños se estiman en 23,7 kilogramos.

facts.statement: The large number of Protoceratops found in high concentrations suggests they lived in herds.
facts.quote: El gran número de estos animales encontrados en grandes concentraciones hace pensar que vivieron en manadas.

facts.statement: Protoceratops was related to Leptoceratops, a ceratopsian that inhabited North America.
facts.quote: Protoceratops estaba emparentado con el Leptoceratops, un ceratopsio que habitaba en Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Some revisions, such as those by Peter Dodson, attribute differences in the size and shape of certain cranial bones, specifically the parietal and squamosal, to sexual dimorphism in addition to age.
facts.quote: Algunas revisiones, como la de Peter Dodson, atribuyen la diferencia de tamaño y forma de algunos huesos craneales, concretamente el parietal y el escamoso, a la existencia de cierto dimorfismo sexual, además de la edad.

facts.statement: Despite its relatively small size, Protoceratops likely had an intimidating appearance due to a solid head shield and a sharp beak in its mouth.
facts.quote: Su aspecto debió ser intimidatorio a pesar de su relativamente pequeño tamaño, ya que su cabeza estaba protegida por una maciza placa y su boca poseía un afilado pico.

facts.statement: Skeleton reconstruction indicates that Protoceratops was a quadruped.
facts.quote: La reconstrucción del esqueleto indica que este animal era cuadrúpedo.

facts.statement: The head shield likely served not only to protect against frontal attacks but also as a display element during the mating season.
facts.quote: La placa, además de proteger de posibles ataques frontales, probablemente fuera un elemento más del cortejo durante el período de apareamiento.

facts.statement: Protoceratops had prominent jaw muscles capable of generating great force, allowing it to tear plants and leaves and then chew them with rows of strong teeth.
facts.quote: Los músculos de la mandíbula eran prominentes, capaces de realizar una gran fuerza. De esta manera era capaz de arrancar las plantas y hojas de las que se alimentaba. Después masticaba los alimentos con sus hileras de fuertes dientes.

facts.statement: Although an herbivore, Protoceratops appears to have had a powerful bite.
facts.quote: Aunque fue un herbívoro, parece haber tenido una poderosa mordida.

facts.statement: The skull ended in a very strong frontal beak and was perforated by four pairs of temporal fenestrae.
facts.quote: El cráneo terminaba en un pico frontal muy fuerte y estaba perforada en cuatro pares de fenestras temporales.

facts.statement: Protoceratops possessed a large eye orbit measuring approximately 50 millimeters in diameter.
facts.quote: También poseía una órbita ocular grande que medía alrededor de 50 milímetros de diámetro.

facts.statement: The frill, consisting mainly of the parietal bone and partially of the squamosal, was perforated by two large parietal fenestrae.
facts.quote: La gola, que consiste sobre todo en el hueso parietal y parcialmente en el escamoso, estaba perforada por dos grandes fenestras parietales.

facts.statement: The exact size and shape of the neck frill varied among individuals; some specimens had short, compact frills while others had frills nearly half the length of the skull.
facts.quote: El tamaño exacto y la forma de la gola del cuello variaban en cada individuo: algunos especímenes tenían golas cortas y compactas, mientras que otros las tenían de una longitud de casi la mitad del cráneo.

facts.statement: In 1922, a scientific expedition led by American explorer Roy Chapman Andrews searching for human ancestors in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia found the first Protoceratops remains.
facts.quote: En 1922 una expedición científica que buscaba a los ancestros humanos en el desierto de Gobi de Mongolia, encabezada por el explorador estadounidense Roy Chapman Andrews, encontró los primeros restos.

facts.statement: The expedition's photographer, J. B. Shackelford, was the one who actually found the remains.
facts.quote: Fue el fotógrafo del grupo, J. B. Shackelford, el que consiguió encontrarlos.

facts.statement: This discovery proved for the first time that dinosaurs were oviparous; previously, although considered reptiles, it was unknown how they reproduced.
facts.quote: Este descubrimiento demostró por primera vez que los dinosaurios eran ovíparos; anteriormente, aunque se considerara que los dinosaurios eran reptiles, no se sabía como se reproducían estos animales.

facts.statement: Walter Granger and W. K. Gregory formally described the type species, P. andrewsi, in 1923, with the specific name honoring Andrews.
facts.quote: Walter Granger y W. K. Gregory describieron formalmente la especie tipo, P. andrewsi, en 1923, cuyo nombre específico es en honor a Andrews.

facts.statement: The remains originated from the Minhe Formation in Gansu Province, Inner Mongolia, China.
facts.quote: Los restos provenían de la Formación Minhe, provincia de Gansu, Mongolia interior, China.

facts.statement: In 1971, a fossil of this dinosaur was found entangled in combat with a Velociraptor in the Djadochta Formation in Omnogov, Mongolia.
facts.quote: En 1971 se encontró un fósil de este dinosaurio entrelazado en combate con un Velociraptor en la Formación Djadochta en Omnogov, Mongolia.

facts.statement: It is believed that both animals died simultaneously while fighting, either when surprised by a sandstorm or when buried when a dune collapsed on them.
facts.quote: Se cree que los dos murieron simultáneamente mientras peleaban, cuando fueron sorprendidos por una tormenta de arena o enterrados cuando una duna se derrumbó encima de ellos.

facts.statement: In 1975, Polish paleontologists Teresa Maryanska and Halszka Osmólska described a second species of Protoceratops from the Campanian of Mongolia, named P. kozlowskii.
facts.quote: En 1975 las paleontólogas polacas Teresa Maryanska y Halszka Osmólska describieron una segunda especie de Protoceratops, del Campaniano de Mongolia, a la que llamaron P. kozlowskii.

facts.statement: However, it consisted of incomplete remains of a juvenile specimen and is now considered a junior synonym of Bagaceratops rozhdestvenskyi.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, consistían en restos incompletos de un ejemplar juvenil, y hoy es considerada sinónimo más moderno de Bagaceratops rozhdestvenskyi.

facts.statement: In 2001, a second valid species, P. hellenikorhinus, was named from the Bayan Mandahu Formation in Inner Mongolia, China, and also dates to the Campanian.
facts.quote: En 2001 fue nombrada una segunda especie válida, P. hellenikorhinus, proveniente de la Formación Bayan Mandahu en Mongolia interior, China y también data del Campaniano.

facts.statement: This species is probably as large as P. andrewsi but has a significantly different frill with more robust jugal horns.
facts.quote: Esta es probablemente tan grande como el P. andrewsi, teniendo una gola significativamente distinta, con cuernos yugales más robustos.

facts.statement: The bone arch over its nasal fenestrae featured two small nasal horns, and there were no teeth at the front of the snout.
facts.quote: El arco del hueso sobre sus fenestras de la nariz presentaba dos pequeños cuernos nasales y no había dientes en el frente del hocico.

facts.statement: In 2011, it was discovered that a Protoceratops specimen originally unearthed in 1965 preserved footprints of the animal, making it the first known dinosaur preserved with footprints.
facts.quote: En 2011 se descubrió que un espécimen de Protoceratops que fue desenterrado originalmente en 1965 preservaba huellas del animal. Es el primer ejemplo conocido de un dinosaurio preservado con huellas.

facts.statement: Protoceratops was the first named protoceratopsid and gave its name to the family Protoceratopsidae, a group of herbivorous dinosaurs that were advanced enough to be psittacosaurids but primitive enough not to be ceratopsids.
facts.quote: Protoceratops fue el primer protoceratópsido nombrado y quien le daría el nombre a la familia Protoceratopsidae, un grupo de dinosaurios herbívoros que fueron muy avanzados también para ser psitacosáuridos, pero primitivos como para ser ceratópsidos.

facts.statement: In 1998, Paul Sereno defined Protoceratopsidae as the node clade including «all ceratopsians more closely related to Protoceratops than to Triceratops».
facts.quote: En 1998 Paul Sereno definió a Protoceratopsidae como el clado nodo vástago que incluye a «todos los coronosaurios más cercanos a Protoceratops que a Triceratops».

facts.statement: In 2006, Makovicky and Norell published a new phylogeny that removed many genera from Protoceratopsidae, along with several other existing phylogenies.
facts.quote: En 2006, Makovicky y Norell publicaron una nueva filogenia en la que quitan a muchos géneros de Protoceratopsidae, además de varias otras filogenias que también existen.

facts.statement: Protoceratops is classified within the dinosaur class Ornithischia.
facts.quote: Class: Ornithischia

facts.statement: Protoceratops lived from 121.4 to 72.2 million years ago, spanning the Aptian to Campanian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Campanian (121.4 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Roy Chapman Andrews discovered the first fossil dinosaur eggs in the Gobi Desert of Mongolia during the 1920s.
facts.quote: En la década del 1920, Roy Chapman Andrews descubrió los primeros huevos fósiles de dinosaurios en el Desierto de Gobi de Mongolia.

facts.statement: Protoceratops eggs were about 20 centimeters in diameter, and newborns were estimated to be 30 centimeters long.
facts.quote: Cada huevo medía alrededor de 20 centímetros de diámetro y la cría recién nacida debía haber medido 30 centímetros de largo.

facts.statement: A nest containing 15 young Protoceratops andrewsi was discovered in Mongolia in 2011.
facts.quote: En 2011, se descubrió un nido de 15 jóvenes Protoceratops andrewsi en Mongolia.

facts.statement: Studies of growth lines in embryonic P. andrewsi teeth suggest a minimum incubation period of 83.16 days.
facts.quote: Los estudios de líneas de crecimiento, es decir, líneas de von Ebner, de los dientes en P. andrewsi embrionario sugieren plesiomórficamente tiempos de incubación prolongados, con un tiempo mínimo de incubación de 83,16 días para P. andrewsi.

facts.statement: Clusters of Protoceratops nests suggest the animals may have lived in herds or family groups.
facts.quote: Igualmente se han encontrado agrupaciones de nidos de Protoceratops, por lo cual es posible que los Protoceratops vivieran en manada o con una organización de tipo familiar.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Protoceratops was nocturnal or catemeral; large eyes suggest nocturnality, but scleral ring comparisons suggest activity during short intervals throughout the day.
facts.quote: Se ha sugerido que los grandes ojos de Protoceratops son evidencia de un estilo de vida nocturno. Sin embargo, las comparaciones posteriores entre los anillos esclerales de Protoceratops y las aves y reptiles modernos han indicado un estilo de vida más catemeral, activo durante todo el día durante intervalos cortos.

facts.statement: In 2016, Mark Witton refuted the hypothesis that Protoceratops fossils inspired the myth of the griffin, arguing it ignores pre-Greek art and accounts.
facts.quote: En 2016, esta hipótesis fue refutada por Mark Witton, ya que ignora el arte y los relatos de los grifos pre-griegos.

facts.statement: Greek writers began describing the griffin around 675 BC, coinciding with their contact with the Scythians.
facts.quote: Los escritores griegos comienzan a describir al grifo alrededor de 675 a. C., al mismo tiempo que tuvieron contacto con los escitas.
